prompt_en: A photographic analog-horror scene centered on a disturbing anomaly within a familiar recorded television signal: the recording turns an ordinary human presence into an unsettling contradiction. The woman from the supplied portrait is a late-night continuity announcer, seated at the narrow desk of a modest public television sign-off booth. Her facial features follow the supplied portrait, and her short black bob with wispy bangs remains recognizable. She wears a softly draped muted ivory blouse with an open collar, carrying a quiet, natural personal presence in the workaday room. She has just stopped reading. Her lips are closed, and her head has turned slightly toward the CRT television beside her; her eyes fix on it with a small, arrested uncertainty. Both forearms rest on the desk, with her relaxed hands lying on the single sign-off script. A tabletop broadcast microphone, acoustic wall panels and a red ON AIR lamp establish the small production space. The lamp remains lit after the sign-off. Place the box-shaped CRT immediately beside her at face height, its glass angled toward the viewer, so her real face and its television counterpart are large enough to compare in one view. The television shows this same woman in the same blouse and booth, staring straight into its recording lens. Her screen counterpart's mouth is stretched into a deep, open oval as if still pronouncing a held syllable, while the physical woman's mouth remains gently closed. The screen's familiar sign-off caption reads GOOD NIGHT. Fine interlaced lines, smeared composite-video color and one rolling horizontal tracking break run across the television face. The disruption belongs visibly to the broadcast image; the desk and physical face retain ordinary photographic detail. Frame a restrained waist-up three-quarter photograph from just across the desk, with the woman's face on the left and the CRT filling much of the right third. Keep both faces and the microphone readable together. A small warm desk light preserves the softness of her cheeks and a faint natural sheen on her closed lips, against the cold television spill and a largely dim booth. Worn beige equipment and shallow pools of light make the situation mundane enough for the contradiction to feel private and wrong. The emotional center is her dawning recognition that the broadcast has continued on its own.
